transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-30
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neil (Redwood SE), Jared Park (Redwood CSM); Priya Rao (Zenlytic Head of ML), Carlos Mendes (Platform Eng), Aisha Khan (SecOps), Noah Kim (Data Scientist)

Optional summary (auto):
- Quick results review from last week's benchmark: mixed latency on long-tail requests, embeddings stable.
- Agreement on a two-tier pin list: critical models pinned to dedicated pool, lower-tier on hosted with soft-fallback.
- Action items: updated catalog, rollout/playbook for rollback, security follow-up.

Topics: model selection, version pinning, rollback playbook, latency vs cost, VPC/security checklist, next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Okay folks, thanks for joining. We're on the weekly POC sync, wanted to focus today on the decisioning wave — which models we pin where and having an explicit rollback playbook. Priya, quick intro?

[00:12] Priya Rao: Yeah thanks Maya, hi everyone. We're here because decisioning latency is a blocker for our fraud detection flow. We got the numbers from last week but we need more deterministic behavior for the high-value path.

[00:25] Carlos Mendes: And to add, our infra team is concerned about burst traffic in PRDs, if we hit any model slowdowns we need an automatic escape hatch.

[00:33] Liam O'Neil: Right. So today we'll walk through a catalog comparison, propose a pin list and cover rapid rollback steps - both soft fallback and hard rollback. I pulled the heatmaps and some percentiles.

[00:45] Noah Kim: one thing, we also have two model families in test: a 13B dense and a 7B quantized. The 13B is better for few-shot reasoning, but cost is 2.4x.

[00:58] Maya Chen: Good callout. Let's go over the short table. Liam, can you summarize the performance delta?

[01:05] Liam O'Neil: Sure. On average, the 13B in dedicated pool P95 is ~220ms for short prompts (<=64 tokens), P99 spikes to ~780ms on certain multi-turn requests. The 7B quantized on hosted is P95 ~140ms, P99 ~420ms. But on longer sequences the 13B's KV cache gives us better sustained throughput which helps the decisioning resume context — but it's expensive.

[01:36] Priya Rao: The problem is our risk scorer uses context windows ~512 tokens. The 7B falls off at 512, we saw hallucinations in ~2% of test cases — that's not acceptable.

[01:48] Carlos Mendes: We need a deterministic SLA for the critical path (orders flagged as high-risk) — ideally under 300ms P95.

[01:56] Maya Chen: That suggests pinning the 13B to Dedicated for that path, and keeping 7B as fallback for lower-risk requests. But we need to specify soft-fallback rules and an emergency rollback.

[02:08] Aisha Khan: From SecOps perspective, if we put 13B on Dedicated we need to confirm KMS integration and that logs for those requests are forwarded to our SIEM. Also need audit logs.

[02:20] Jared Park: We can surface per-request routing tags and attach them to your audit logs - Redwood Console supports that. I'll own mapping event keys to your SIEM.

[02:30] Maya Chen: Great. Now, Liam, can you talk through the catalog comparison doc you sent and the proposed pin tiers?

[02:38] Liam O'Neil: Absolutely. I made three tiers: Tier A (Critical): 13B-optim-dedicated v1.2 pinned; Tier B (Primary fallback): 7B-quantized hosted v2.0; Tier C (Cost-saver): 3B distilled hosted v1.0 for bulk non-critical scoring. The idea is route critical requests to Tier A always; if Tier A latency exceeds threshold or capacity event happens, soft-fallback to Tier B with partial context trimming; if both Tier A and B fail, route to Tier C with a degraded response template and immediate alerting.

[03:18] Priya Rao: The trimming strategy worries me — if you trim context we might lose signals and scores change. Can we instead do selective field hashing — only send essential tokens?

[03:27] Liam O'Neil: Yes, selective prefixing — send the static user features + last 128 tokens. We'll document which fields are essential.

[03:34] Noah Kim: Also, what about model pinning at inference level vs pinning by route? We have two services calling the models, would it be per-route pin or account-wide?

[03:44] Maya Chen: We usually recommend route-level pinning for flexibility — you can evolve non-critical routes separately. For your case, pin the fraud_decision route to Tier A while keeping other routes on the hosted catalog.

[03:55] Carlos Mendes: Ok but we also want an automated circuit breaker if P99 exceeds X ms for Y minutes. Do you support that?

[04:03] Liam O'Neil: Yes, Redwood has policy-based routing. You can set rules: if P99 > 600ms for 5 minutes on a pod, mark the pool degraded and route new requests to fallback. We can also do soft-fallback where we shadow traffic to observe quality before switching.

[04:20] Priya Rao: Shadowing would help. Can we shadow 10% of traffic to the fallback while still serving from Tier A?

[04:26] Liam O'Neil: Yep, split traffic is supported. You can do weighted split and automatic rollback if error budgets are breached.

[04:34] Maya Chen: Let's walk through an emergency rollback playbook — Liam, you mentioned CLI commands earlier, can you outline?

[04:41] Liam O'Neil: Short version: 1) Trigger a pool drain for the model version (redwoodctl pool drain --pool=dedicated-13b-v1.2 --grace=30s), 2) Switch route pin (redwoodctl route update --route=fraud_decision --model=7b-quantized-v2.0 --mode=soft), 3) Set alerting and incident status, 4) Roll forward once root cause fixed. I will produce a one-pager with exact CLI and UI steps.

[05:03] Carlos Mendes: Does redwoodctl support RBAC? We don't want any engineer to run those commands.

[05:10] Liam O'Neil: Yes, RBAC and SSO integration. We can map roles to allowed commands and require MFA for production actions.

[05:18] Aisha Khan: Great. Also need to confirm that pool drain will stream in-flight requests to finish — we can't drop in-flight scoring.

[05:26] Liam O'Neil: Pool drain has a grace window and will allow inflight tokens to finish. We recommend a 30-60s grace depending on request size.

[05:33] Maya Chen: Good. Now on the catalog cost side — Priya asked earlier about unit economics. Maya to present cost numbers?

[05:40] Maya Chen: Quick numbers: 13B dedicated unit, per-1M tokens cost ~ $86 on dedicated reserved, 7B quantized hosted ~ $35 per-1M tokens, 3B distilled ~ $12 per-1M. Those are illustrative — we'll attach a spreadsheet with exact math per your expected QPS.

[05:59] Priya Rao: That delta is big. We'll need to justify Dedicated spend by showing the revenue impact of preventing false negatives on high-risk cases.

[06:08] Noah Kim: We can run an A/B for a week, route a small percentage of high-value sessions to Tier A and estimate lift.

[06:16] Maya Chen: Absolutely. Also note Dedicated offers better tail latency and consistent variance.

[06:22] Carlos Mendes: On the topic of variance, Liam you mentioned KV cache behavior. We saw earlier that performance regresses after cold starts — can we warm the cache?

[06:31] Liam O'Neil: Yes, you can pre-warm with synthetic prompts or a small warm pool. We also support sticky sessions to benefit KV cache locality. We'll give recommended warm-up scripts.

[06:40] Aisha Khan: Anything about data residency? For Dedicated, if it's in our VPC region, we need to ensure the private control plane meets our compliance.

[06:47] Jared Park: For private deployments we support VPC peering or on-prem packages. And Redwood's audit trail can be configured to retain logs for a year if needed. We'll share SOC-2 and ISO artifacts.

[06:58] Priya Rao: On fallbacks, I'm concerned about silent degradations — e.g., fallback returns different score distributions without obvious errors. How do we detect regressions?

[07:08] Liam O'Neil: Good question. Redwood Optimize can run evaluation sets against both primary and fallback and surface quality delta metrics. We can wire regression alerts that trigger when a key metric deviates by X%. Shadowing traffic with logging is also recommended to compute live deltas.

[07:23] Maya Chen: We'll attach a suggested eval set — Noah, can you confirm you can provide 200 annotated examples for a live regression harness?

[07:30] Noah Kim: Yes, we can pull 200 cases focusing on high-risk flows. We'll label the expected scores.

[07:36] Maya Chen: Awesome. Now let's talk timelines and cutover criteria. Our recommendation is staged: week 1 — pin Tier A to a small fraction of users (5-10%) and shadow 20% to Tier B; week 2 — increase to 50% after verifying metrics; week 3 — full roll. If any metric breaches — latency, error-rate or quality delta — run the rollback playbook.

[08:02] Carlos Mendes: Can we automate the increase with safety gates?

[08:06] Liam O'Neil: Yes, Redwood supports automated ramp with SLO gates. We'll provide a template.

[08:11] Priya Rao: One more operational ask: we need a dry-run of a rollback. Can we schedule a tabletop next week and practice the commands?

[08:19] Maya Chen: Definitely. Jared, can you coordinate a 45-minute tabletop next Wednesday?

[08:25] Jared Park: Yup, I'll propose times and include the ops doc.

[08:29] Aisha Khan: For the security follow-up, I want to confirm that KMS keys will be customer-managed and that logs obfuscate PII tokens. Also need to see encryption-in-transit proof.

[08:40] Liam O'Neil: Customer-managed KMS supported; we also have token redaction hooks for logs. I'll note the exact controls in the security pack we'll send.

[08:49] Maya Chen: Great. A few quick clarifications from earlier messages. Priya — you mentioned hallucinations with the 7B; what's the tolerance on false positives vs false negatives?

[08:58] Priya Rao: For high-risk, false negatives (missed fraud) are expensive — we want under 0.5% FN. FP we can tune later.

[09:06] Noah Kim: We'll design the eval to be FN-focused.

[09:10] Carlos Mendes: On instrumentation, include request IDs and model version in every trace so we can backtrace which model produced a given score.

[09:17] Jared Park: That's standard — we'll ensure trace metadata includes request_id, model_id, pool_id, and routing_reason.

[09:24] Maya Chen: Okay wrapping to next steps. To repeat: Maya will send the updated catalog + cost spreadsheet, Liam will produce rollback playbook and CLI steps, Carlos will run latency stress tests and export traces, Aisha and Jared will align on KMS/SIEM mapping and schedule security follow-up. Noah will provide the 200-case eval set.

[09:45] Priya Rao: One more, can you include a short note on when Dedicated vs Private (on-prem) makes sense? Our compliance team might prefer private if we escalate.

[09:54] Maya Chen: We'll add a decision matrix: Hosted for day 0 quickstart, Dedicated for predictable high-throughput and tail latency with tenant isolation, Private if you need full control over network/data plane or air-gapped compliance.

[10:06] Carlos Mendes: Are there any competitive notes we should be aware of? We were evaluating Anthropic for a similar stack — any major differences in routing or enterprise controls?

[10:15] Liam O'Neil: Anthropic provides strong model safety but their enterprise routing and automated fallback primitives aren't as mature for multi-pool soft-fallbacks. OpenAI has hosted reliability but less configuration for dedicated fleet orchestration. We'll include a short competitor comparison slide.

[10:31] Maya Chen: All right that's about it. Quick recap of action items and deadlines — Maya to send catalog by 7/31, Liam rollback doc by 8/02, Carlos traces by 8/03, Aisha KMS list by 8/05, Jared schedule tabletop next Wednesday, Noah deliver eval cases by 8/02.

[10:52] Priya Rao: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[10:56] Maya Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with links. Sharing: meeting deck (link), catalog spreadsheet (link), security pack (link).

[11:04] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings; speaker labels mostly accurate but sometimes roles collapsed into names.
